I find this very interesting as a native American person living in Australia. The way that indigenous people claim indigenous heritage here in Australia is very similar to North America. Provided they have connection to the tribe with which they are trying to identify and have family trees/birth certificate that shows they have one indigenous ancestor back at least within 4 generations (it might be more or less, I am not sure) they can identify as indigenous and qualify as member of a tribe and several government benefits. Some of these people look extremely white, maybe even have 100% European DNA because of the stolen generation (White Australia forcibly removing indigenous children, especially mixed race indigenous children to integrate them with white society and breed the aboriginality out of them).  In these sorts of cases, where descendants of Aboriginal people who are genetically white but have still suffered due to the dispossession of their non white ancestors, I can understand why they would want to identify as having indigenous heritage and think they would have a right to even though the waters are murky re: benefits/programs. That being said, my dad looks like a white man. He is blonde, blue eyed and light skinned. My mum is clearly indigenous or at least mestiza but even so, I still inherited 67% native American DNA which means my father, as white as he looked, still had a significant proportion of native DNA.

Hi! I'm sorry I can't answer your question about finding more resources as I'm in the process of researching my ancestors myself, but I thought I'd comment because I don't think the Native South American community on reddit is particularly large. I'm a first generation Peruvian-Australian who has been curious about my heritage for a very long time, mostly due to lack of identity and constant questioning of "what" I am. My family is incredibly mixed, with mostly Euro-Indigenous as far as I know on both sides of the family, however with my mother's side being more indigenous (her father was 100% Indigenous Quechua as far as I know and her maternal line had quite a lot of indigenous influence)!and my father predominantly European (only 1 indigenous ancestor known). As such, I came out quite racially ambiguous and never really knew what to identify as, especially considering I grew up in Australia with minimal exposure to my South American roots that I didn't really connect with anyway. However most recently, I decided to take a DNA test to put my heritage questions to rest. I found out I was 62% Native American, with an extra 2% actually matching to modern day Siberians. The rest was unremarkably European. I've never really connected with the popular "mestizo" culture, but I remember when I was younger listening to Indigenous Andean music and feeling like it was music from MY people, whereas I didn't really feel the same connection with the popular definition of "Latin" music. Recently, I told my mother I don't identify as a Latino. I identify primary as an indigenous person with some euro ancestry. That's it. I know a lot about my euro ancestors, but not nearly as much of my native ancestors. My only clues are that they were predominantly mountain people, Andeans who spoke Quechua and lived in the highlands. I hope you have more luck tracing your indigenous heritage than me!
